title: H-1B Worker's Immigration Anxiety Becomes the App Visawise
excerpt: Kadambi built an app to manage life on a work visa — status tracking, rental and tax guidance — in the toughest year the H-1B program has faced.
body:
• Kadambi, an H-1B visa holder, built Visawise — an app with an H-1B status banner and immigration-relevant rental, vehicle, and tax guidance — to manage the anxiety of living on a work visa.
  • The app is a personal response to a punishing year for H-1B workers: a $100,000 visa fee, tightened interviews, and the 60-day layoff grace period, with Indians making up 71% of approvals.
  • He is explicit about the app's limits: the rules logic has not yet been reviewed by an immigration attorney or CPA, and disclaimers run throughout the product.
  • The fee that drove much of the anxiety was struck down by a federal judge in June 2026 — but DHS has proposed making a $103,265 version permanent.

Kadambi is an H-1B worker who got tired of the anxiety. Instead of refreshing case trackers and immigration forums, he built an app — Visawise — to manage life on a work visa, The American Bazaar reported this week. The app combines an H-1B status banner with practical guidance for visa holders: immigration-relevant information on renting, vehicles, and taxes, with disclaimers throughout that the rules logic has not yet been formally reviewed by an immigration attorney or a CPA.

"Bringing in actual professional review, an immigration attorney checking the rules logic, a CPA looking at the tax-related sections, is something I'd genuinely like to do as this grows. It's not something I can claim has already happened, and I'd rather say that plainly than let the disclaimers do the work of hiding that gap," he told The American Bazaar.

Anxiety as a product spec

Kadambi frames his measure of success not in users or growth charts but in anxiety removed. "Honestly, success for me isn't a user count or a growth chart. It's whether the people actually using it a year from now would say it removed real anxiety from their lives, the same anxiety I described at the start of this conversation," he said. He plans to explore LLM and WhatsApp custom-agent integrations kept "user-controlled," and hopes to serve a population beyond H-1B and H-4 holders — but only when the rules can be handled responsibly.

The year that made it necessary

On September 19, 2025, President Trump signed a proclamation imposing an additional $100,000 fee on new H-1B applications, with implementation set barely 36–48 hours later — triggering panic as TCS, Microsoft, Amazon, JPMorgan, and Eli Lilly told H-1B staff abroad to return by the deadline. The White House later clarified the fee would not apply to existing holders or renewals. In August 2026, the Department of Homeland Security proposed making the fee permanent at $103,265 — projected to raise $8.8 billion over a decade — with public comment running through September 24. A Blind poll of 1,584 professionals found one in six Indian H-1B holders — or someone they knew — received a deportation Notice to Appear within the 60-day layoff grace period, sometimes in as little as two weeks.

"A $100,000 toll on a bridge of talent will hurt both sides of that bridge. If tariff is tax on goods, this toll on H-1B is a tax on trust."

— Syed Akbaruddin, former Indian Permanent Representative to the UN

Indians at the center of it

India is by far the largest beneficiary of the H-1B program, accounting for 71% of approved beneficiaries, with China second at 11.7%, according to U.S. government data via Reuters. Top H-1B employers include Amazon (10,044 approvals), TCS (5,505), Microsoft (5,189), Meta (5,123), Apple (4,202), and Google (4,181) through June 2025. That exposure has fed a "brain drain to brain gain" debate in India. "Previously, we used to call it brain drain; now we can look at it as brain gain," Akbaruddin said, arguing that global capability centers can become "India's H-1B visa." Others are skeptical: most H-1B holders have homes, families, and stability in the U.S., and reverse migration is likely limited to a small entrepreneurial group.

What comes next

The legal picture is still moving. On June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin struck down the $100,000 fee, ruling that "the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," and the First Circuit refused to block that ruling in July while the government appeals. Only about 85 employers had actually paid the fee as of February 2026. But the administration is moving to codify the fee permanently through rulemaking, with DHS's $103,265 proposal potentially finalized by year-end. For Kadambi, the product is the point either way: the rules will keep changing, and someone has to translate them into a life that still works.
image_caption: Karthik Kadambi, the H-1B worker who built the Visawise app.
nri_angle: With Indians making up 71% of H-1B approvals, a diaspora-built tool for visa anxiety is a direct response to the policy shocks hitting Indian workers hardest this year.
author: Diaspora Desk
